title: Mangroves

names.gloss: species of mangrove with a long thin fruit, soaked to make it edible
species of mangrove with a short thin fruit, leached of its poison
species of mangrove whose hard wood is good for oars

identification.basis: The dictionary names six mangroves by their fruit, wood or sap without botanical names; the matches here to the orange mangrove (eaten after leaching), the cannonball mangrove (oars) and the blind-your-eye mangrove (poisonous sap) follow Anderson's and Roth's identifications of the same uses.

summary: The dictionary has a mangrove for every use and no botany: **[kajul](word:kajul)**, 'a long thin fruit which must be soaked in water to make it edible'; **[kakaji](word:kakaji)**, 'a short thin fruit which becomes edible by leaching out the poison'; **[marril](word:marril)**, 'with apple-like seed only much bigger. The wood is hard and is good for making oars'; **[miyilabu](word:miyilabu)**, 'a poisonous sap which makes people blind'; **[kurubarr](word:kurubarr)** and **[kurunkal](word:kurunkal)** 'with a long round seed'; and **[mangkurru](word:mangkurru)**, the English word borrowed [ref:hershberger1982]. Those are, in order, the orange mangrove whose green propagules are 'eaten after scraping, washing, drying and cooking to remove tannins' across the north, the cannonball mangrove *Xylocarpus* that Anderson's informants made paddles from, and the blind-your-eye mangrove *Excoecaria* whose latex 'can cause temporary blindness' and whose smoke Kuku Yalanji said does the same [ref:wiki-bruguiera] [ref:anderson1996] [ref:wiki-excoecaria]. The mangroves are the Bloomfield's larder and hardware store: the [mud crab](entry:mud-crab), the [oysters](entry:oysters) on the roots, the mangrove worm in the dead trunks, the [stingray](entry:stingrays) on the flats, the harpoon shaft of *Rhizophora*, and the canoe hull of the milky mangrove on the Endeavour [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1910]. This is a page of the sea country of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji, the Bloomfield and Daintree coast; it is a long way from [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) on the upper Mitchell, and is here because the words, the trade and the tools reach inland. On the Mitchell the nearest mangroves are at its mouth, two hundred kilometres downstream; the river's 'freshwater mangrove' is a different tree, on the [fish poison plants](entry:fish-poison-plants) page.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[mangkurru](word:mangkurru)** 'mangrove (english loan word)'. **[kajul](word:kajul)** 'species of mangrove. A long thin fruit which must be soaked in water to make it edible'. **[kakaji](word:kakaji)** 'species of mangrove with a short thin fruit which becomes edible by leaching out the poison'. **[marril](word:marril)** 'species of mangrove, with apple-like seed only much bigger. The wood is hard and is good for making oars'. **[miyilabu](word:miyilabu)** 'species of mangrove. It has a poisonous sap which makes people blind'. **[kurubarr](word:kurubarr)** and **[kurunkal](word:kurunkal)** 'species of mangrove with a long round seed'. **[walbul-walbul](word:walbul-walbul)** is, among other things, 'species of mangrove, long round seed' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Endeavour River canoe timbers include the 'milky mangrove' *Excoecaria agallocha* and *Sonneratia*, and the Bloomfield turtle-harpoon shaft was the mangrove *Rhizophora apiculata* [ref:roth1910] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: The mangroves and their uses
sections.body:
**Red or spotted mangrove** (*Rhizophora stylosa*): 'a small to medium-sized evergreen tree ... up to 15 metres tall', on stilt roots, with dark bark and pear-shaped fruit that sprouts on the tree [ref:wiki-rhizophora]. Its straight poles were the Bloomfield harpoon shaft, 'up to three metres long made from the mangrove *Rhizophora apiculata*' [ref:anderson1996].

**Grey mangrove** (*Avicennia marina*): 'a shrub or tree to a height of 3 to 10 m, or up to 14 metres in tropical regions', with 'smooth light-grey bark made up of thin, stiff, brittle flakes' and thick leaves 'silvery-white, or grey' beneath, standing in a field of pencil roots; 'a pioneer in muddy soil' [ref:wiki-avicennia].

**Orange mangrove** (*Bruguiera gymnorhiza*), *kajul* or *kakaji*: 'a mangrove tree that grows usually to 7–20 metres high', 'found on the seaward side of mangrove swamps, often in the company of *Rhizophora*'. 'The fruit (propagule/hypocotyl) is reported as being eaten after scraping/grating, washing, drying and cooking to remove tannins'; 'the green propagules/hypocotyls are also eaten by many indigenous groups in northern Australia. For example, on northwestern Cape York Peninsula, in the Weipa region, Thaynakwithi people' eat them. 'The wood is widely used, including for firewood, building construction ... canoe parts, fishing stakes, spears' [ref:wiki-bruguiera]. The dictionary's two leached mangrove fruits are on the [leaching](entry:leaching) page, with Roth's sand-basin method [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].

**Yellow mangrove** (*Ceriops tagal*): 'a medium-sized tree growing to a height of 25 metres', buttressed, with 'silvery-grey to orangish-brown' bark and glossy yellowish leaves; 'favoured as firewood, being second only to *Rhizophora*', and 'its bark and sap yield red and black dyes' and tannin [ref:wiki-ceriops].

**Blind-your-eye or milky mangrove** (*Excoecaria agallocha*), *miyilabu*: 'The milky latex of *Excoecaria agallocha* is very poisonous and powerfully irritant ... Contact with skin causes irritation and rapid blistering; slight contact with eyes can cause temporary blindness, hence the common names that refer to blindness. Even the generic name is from the Latin for "blinder"'. 'Burning the wood can release toxic fumes in the smoke leading to eye irritation'; 'even dried and powdered leaves retain the poison and can kill fish quickly' [ref:wiki-excoecaria]. Anderson: 'a mangrove species, *Excoecaria agallocha*, produces a smoke which is said by Kuku-Yalanji to produce blindness' [ref:anderson1996]. Roth found its light wood in the Endeavour River dug-outs [ref:roth1910].

**Cannonball mangrove** (*Xylocarpus granatum*), *marril*: the paddle wood, 'paddles were made from *Xylocarpus granatum*', with the big round fruit the dictionary describes as an apple-like seed 'only much bigger' [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

**The mangrove's animals.** The mud crab, the mangrove worm in the dead logs, the oysters on the roots and rocks, the mullet and bream and barramundi of the creeks, the stingrays on the flats, and the saltwater crocodile; the Traditional Owners' plan calls the mangrove and mudflat areas 'very important breeding areas' for fish and shellfish [ref:anderson1996] [ref:jabalbina2016]. The [mud crab](entry:mud-crab) page has the flats.

sections.heading: Telling the mangroves apart
sections.body:
- **Stilt roots** arching from the trunk: red mangrove [ref:wiki-rhizophora].
- **Pencil roots** standing up out of the mud in a field, pale flaky bark, silver leaf undersides: grey mangrove [ref:wiki-avicennia].
- **Knee roots** looping out of the mud, big leaves, a long cigar propagule: orange mangrove, the food one [ref:wiki-bruguiera].
- **Buttresses and yellow-green glossy leaves**: yellow mangrove, the firewood [ref:wiki-ceriops].
- **Milky sap when a leaf is broken, and leaves that turn red before they fall**: blind-your-eye; never into the eyes, never on the fire [ref:wiki-excoecaria].
- **A fruit like a cannonball** hanging from a smooth-barked tree: cannonball mangrove, the oar wood [ref:hershberger1982].
- **The river's 'freshwater mangrove'** at Karma Waters is *Barringtonia*, a fish-poison tree, not one of these [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Mud-crab holes** under the roots at low tide; see [mud crab](entry:mud-crab) [ref:anderson1996].
- **Oysters** cemented on the roots and the rocks at the creek mouths [ref:wiki-saccostrea].
- **Dead mangrove trunks soft with worm**: the mangrove worm [ref:anderson1996].
- **A slide and a drag** on the mud bank: the crocodile [ref:crocwise].
- **Propagules sprouting on the tree** and washed up along the strand [ref:wiki-rhizophora] [ref:wiki-bruguiera].

sections.heading: Where they grow
sections.body: The tidal creeks and river mouths of the coast, the Bloomfield's 'mangrove areas at the mouth and on the several islands in the Bloomfield River', the grey mangrove furthest up the creeks and furthest south, the red mangrove and the orange mangrove toward the sea [ref:anderson1996] [ref:wiki-avicennia] [ref:wiki-bruguiera]. On the Mitchell the mangroves are at its mouth on the Gulf, Kokoberra and Yir Yoront country [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: The nursery
sections.body: The mangroves hold the mud, feed the creeks with leaf fall, and shelter the young of the fish, the crabs and the prawns; the Traditional Owners' plan names them 'very important breeding areas' [ref:jabalbina2016]. Everything on this coast's food pages comes through them: the [mud crab](entry:mud-crab), the [oysters](entry:oysters), the [stingrays](entry:stingrays), the [barramundi](entry:barramundi) and mullet of the creeks, the [sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle) that eats mangrove fruit, and the [saltwater crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile) that eats everything else [ref:gbrmpa-turtles] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The mangrove flats were worked at low tide (*ngajal*) through the year; mullet ran into the creeks in the late dry; the mangrove fruits were leached when gathered; harpoon shafts and canoe timber were cut with the other timber after the storms [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Food**: orange-mangrove propagules leached and cooked (*kajul*, *kakaji*); mangrove worms; and everything that lives among the roots [ref:wiki-bruguiera] [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Harpoon shafts** of *Rhizophora* 'up to three metres long' [ref:anderson1996].
- **Paddles** of cannonball mangrove, *marril* [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Canoe hulls** of milky mangrove and *Sonneratia* on the Endeavour [ref:roth1910].
- **Firewood**: yellow and red mangrove, never blind-your-eye [ref:wiki-ceriops] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Dye and tannin** from yellow-mangrove bark [ref:wiki-ceriops].
- **Fish poison**: the blind-your-eye's leaves 'can kill fish quickly'; see [fish poison plants](entry:fish-poison-plants) [ref:wiki-excoecaria].

sections.heading: Leaching mangrove fruit
sections.body:
From the dictionary, Roth and the Cape York record [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-bruguiera]:

1. **Gather the green propagules** of the orange mangrove, the long cigar-shaped sprouts, from the tree or the strand [ref:wiki-bruguiera].
2. **Scrape or grate** them, and **wash** in changes of water, or soak them in a basin dug in the sand by the swamp, as Roth saw along the coast, 'to leach out the poison' [ref:wiki-bruguiera] [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].
3. **Dry and cook** them; the tannins are what the washing removes [ref:wiki-bruguiera].
4. The [leaching](entry:leaching) page has the general method and the sand-basin.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Blind-your-eye mangrove: no sap in the eyes, no leaves rubbed on skin, no wood on the cooking fire [ref:wiki-excoecaria] [ref:anderson1996].
- Mangrove creeks are the saltwater crocodile's; Be Crocwise [ref:crocwise].
- Mangroves are protected marine plants in Queensland under the *Fisheries Act 1994*; cutting them needs a permit, and the Traditional Owners' plan and the Marine Park rules apply on sea country [ref:qld-fishact] [ref:jabalbina2016] [ref:gbrmpa-tu].
- Oyster shell cuts; boots on the flats.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The Eastern Kuku Yalanji's plan for their country names the mangroves and mudflats as breeding areas to protect, and the rangers at Wujal Wujal patrol them [ref:jabalbina2016] [ref:handback2021]. The dictionary's six mangroves are the useful ones; which botanical trees they are, beyond the three matched here, is for the people who use them [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[mangkurru](word:mangkurru)* 'mangrove'; *[kajul](word:kajul)*, *[kakaji](word:kakaji)* mangroves with leached fruit; *[marril](word:marril)* the oar-wood mangrove; *[miyilabu](word:miyilabu)* the blinding mangrove; *[kurubarr](word:kurubarr)*, *[kurunkal](word:kurunkal)* mangroves with a long round seed; *[ngajal](word:ngajal)* 'low tide'; *[bilngkumu](word:bilngkumu)* 'salt water crocodile'; *[nganjamu](word:nganjamu)* 'worm' [ref:hershberger1982].
